# References to mine — reviewing-conceptual-integrity

## From category #44

### Key references

- **Fred Brooks — *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975; anniversary ed. 1995)** → mine: the source claim, that conceptual integrity is the most important consideration in system design, and its uncomfortable corollary — it is better to omit anomalous features than to include many good but uncoordinated ideas. The reviewable transfer is not the corollary (a review cannot decide what to omit) but its premise: *coherence is a property worth spending features on*, which is what licenses raising it at all. Also the **second-system effect** — the tendency to pile onto a successor everything the first system left out. Cited by title; no URL asserted.
- **Eric Evans — *Domain-Driven Design* (2003)** → mine: the two ideas that make the vocabulary half checkable. **Ubiquitous language** — one term per concept, shared by code, UI, docs, and conversation, so a second name for an existing idea is a defect in the language rather than a matter of taste. And **bounded context** — the counterweight that keeps the check honest: the same word legitimately means different things in different contexts, so a term that differs *across a named boundary* is not a finding. Name the context or drop the objection.
- **Thomas Green & Marian Petre — "Usability analysis of visual programming environments: a 'cognitive dimensions' framework" (*Journal of Visual Languages and Computing*, 1996)** → mine: the framework's **consistency** dimension states this lens's question better than the folk formulations do — *when some of the system has been learnt, how much of the rest can be inferred?* That is a question about a specific change (does what the user already learned still predict this?), not about aesthetics. Adjacent dimensions worth borrowing when they fit: **role-expressiveness** (is it apparent what each part is for) and **hidden dependencies** (a relationship the user must know but cannot see). `(verify — exact dimension list against the paper; the framework has been revised in later work)`
- **Donald Norman — the *system image* (*The Design of Everyday Things*)** → mine: the designer's model and the user's model never meet; the **system image** — everything the product actually shows — is the only channel between them. This is the cleanest statement of the `#42`/`#44` boundary: `#42` reviews whether a person can operate what the image shows, `#44` whether the image still implies one coherent model. A change alters the image whether or not anyone intended a model change.
- **Rich Hickey — "Simple Made Easy" (Strange Loop, 2011)** → mine: **simple** (one fold, one role — an objective property of a thing) versus **easy** (familiar, near at hand — relative to the observer). The transfer: "does this braid a new concept together with an existing one" is a *simplicity* question with an objective answer, which is what separates a reportable finding here from a preference. Cited by title; no URL asserted.
- **Google's API Improvement Proposals (`aip.dev`)** → mine: an existence proof that concept-level consistency across a large surface can be written down as rules rather than left to taste — standard resource shapes, standard method names, standard field semantics, applied uniformly so a new endpoint that invents its own model is *wrong* rather than merely unusual. Where the product is an API, this is the closest thing to a checkable model. `(verify — specific AIP numbers against current site)`
- **`#11 checking-restraint` — the sibling this is most often confused with, and the pairing that matters.** Both push back on additions, and they push back for different reasons: restraint says *don't build it yet*, `#44` says *if you build it, something else is now wrong*. The second is not a weaker form of the first — it applies to changes restraint has no objection to (small, requested, well-scoped) and stays silent on changes restraint blocks (a speculative abstraction with no user-facing concept at all).
